We present new paleomagnetic and isotopic data from the Transantarctic Mountains in East Antarctica that con- strain the paleogeographic position of this region during the late Early and Middle Cambrian. Two new poles have been determined from volcanic and granitic rocks in the Scott Gla- cier area. The first pole is from the Wyatt and Ackerman For- mations (-525 Ma) and the Mount Paine tonalite (40øE, IøN, A95= 6 ø (error circle at the 95% confidence level), N=11 VGPs). The second pole is from the Zanuck granite (36øE, 7øS, A95= 9 ø, N=9 VGPs). These poles differ from the Gondwana early Paleozoic reference poles and could indicate that the Scott Glacier area (and by geologic correlation, north Victoria Land, eastern Australia, and West Antarctica?) was part of a terrane accreted to East Gondwana in the Cambrian. Another possibility is that these new poles support rapid apparent po- lar wander in the late Early Cambrian and Middle Cambrian. This apparent polar wander event could be related to rapid plate motions or to a true polar wander event. The characteristic high-temperature component resides in both haematite and magnetite. Received 1999 May 12; in original form 1998 September 30 SUMMARY A total of 239 orientated drill-core samples from 23 sites were collected for palaeo- magnetic study from Silurian and Devonian red beds, marlaceous sandstone, and limestone rocks in the eastern part of the Hexi Corridor, southwest Ningxia, North China. The characteristic high-temperature component resides in both haematite and magnetite. It clusters around a northwesterly and shallow to moderate downward direction and its antipode after tilt correction. The primary origin of this characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) is ascertained by positive fold and reversal tests at the 95 per cent conﬁdence level. The corresponding palaeopoles, at 339.0°E, 60.1°N with A95=11.2° (Silurian) and 336.0°E, 56.0°N with A95=9.2° (Devonian), imply that the North China Block (NCB) had a low palaeolatitude of around 15°N in the Northern Hemisphere during the Silurian–Devonian period. Comparison with the Early– Middle Ordovician palaeopole of the NCB suggests that the NCB moved rapidly northwards by 30.8°± 10.9° to cross the palaeo-equator during the Early–Middle Ordovician to Silurian. Received 1999 September 13; in original form 1998 July 10 SUMMARY We report on a detailed palaeomagnetic study of the Miocene Farellones volcanic formation in the Chilean Andes near Santiago (two sections, 37 sites, about 400 orientated cores). Petrological observations show evidence of low-grade metamorphism increasing downwards through the volcanic sequence. Optical observations of opaque minerals and magnetic experiments suggest that in many cases maghemitization is associated with hydrothermal alteration. However, thermal demagnetization data indicate that the low-grade metamorphism did not signiﬁcantly modify the direction of the primary remanent magnetization recorded at the time of emplacement of the volcanic lava ﬂows. Four intervals of polarity with two intermediate palaeodirections were observed in the ~650-m-thick composite section. According to the dispersion of ﬂow average directions, palaeosecular variation was slightly larger than that observed in general during the Upper Cenozoic. However, determination of pre-Devonian palaeogeographic evolution of Patagonia will requireacquisitionofnewpalaeomagneticpoles. Conclusions A palaeomagnetic study on the Silurian–Early Devonian sediments of the Sierra Grande Formation, exposed in NE Patagonia, indicated that these rocks are carriers of a syntec- tonic magnetization acquired during the late stages of folding of the sequence. Unblocking temperatures, some rock mag- netic experiments and optical microscopy indicated that ﬁne grain hematite residing in the cement of the sandstones is the onlymagneticcarrier.Thepositionofthepalaeomagneticpole suggests that magnetization and therefore folding occurred during late Early to Late Permian times. Previously obtained Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic poles from Patagonia agree with those from Gondwana since Devonian times, suggesting that if Patagonia is a far-travelled terrane accretion must have occurred before Devonian. Therefore, any tectonic model explaining deformation around the northern boundary of Patagonia as a product of continent–continent collision must account for deformation occurring more than 100Ma after begining of collision.

Dacitic welded tuffs ranging from 24 to 21 Ma possess westerly paleomagnetic directions with normal polarity (formation-mean: D/I = 294.5°/44.2° with α95 = 8.3°, 8 sites), while the andesite flows formed at 17 Ma exhibit southerly directions with reversed polarity (D/I = 186.6°/–61.9°, 2 sites). A positive conglomerate test assures the stability of high-temperature components of remanent magnetization. Our results demonstrate that northern NE Japan rotated counter-clockwise through more than 60 ° between 21 and 17 Ma, most likely in association with the opening of the Japan Sea. The rotation of northern NE Japan thus preceded the about 15 Ma rapid clockwise rotation of SW Japan, and was synchronous with the possible pre-16 Ma southward translation of it. In c

rial volcanic rocks older than 16 Ma. Our newly- obtained data indicate that the area underwent counter- clockwise rotation of more than 60° between 21 and 17 Ma. Taken into consideration with published paleomagnetic data from other areas, we will discuss the amount and timing of counter-clockwise rotation of NE Japan and Early to Middle Miocene intra-arc differential rotations. 2. Geology, Sampling and Tilt Correction Figures 1 and 2 show a simplified geological map and the generalized stratigraphy of the Lower to Middle Miocene sequence of the Ninohe area, respectively. The Lower to Middle Miocene strata are divided into the following four formations in ascending order; the Nisatai Dacite, Yotsuyaku Formation, Kadonosawa Formation, and Suenomatsuyama Formation. The Yotsuyaku Formation intercalates andesitic volcanic rocks, called the Keiseitoge Andesite, within the middle part. For details of lithostratigraphy and paleontol- ogy, refer to Matsubara (1995) and references therein. As a pilot study, one specimen per site was chosen for the progressive thermal demagnetization (PThD) analysis. In this study alternating field demagnetization was not applied as in our experience thermal demagnetization is in general more appropriate to effectively demagnetize high-coercivity magnetization in felsic to intermediate volcanic materials. Dacitic welded tuffs ranging from 24 to 21 Ma possess westerly paleomagnetic directions with normal polarity (formation-mean: D/I = 294.5°/44.2° with α95 = 8.3°, 8 sites), while the andesite flows formed at 17 Ma exhibit southerly directions with reversed polarity (D/I = 186.6°/–61.9°, 2 sites). The Lower to Middle Miocene strata are divided into the following four formations in ascending order; the Nisatai Dacite, Yotsuyaku Formation, Kadonosawa Formation, and Suenomatsuyama Formation. The texture, mineralogy and geochemistry of the saprolith zone are ascribable to primary weathering in part modi®ed by diagenetic reactions. An overlying, crudely bedded breccia at the base of the Lorrain Formation is 4 m thick. The lower 2 m comprises angular clasts 1±30 cm in length of locally derived dacite set in a matrix containing granitic detritus. Two samples from this lower brec- cia zone contain 3.79% and 4.94% Fe 2O3, 0.33% and 0.78% FeO, and 8.70% and 7.40% K 2O [30]. Sokolov Geological Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences, Pyzhevsky per . 7, Moscow 109017, Russia Received 10 May 1999; accepted 20 August 1999 Abstract Mesozoic island-arc and oceanic volcanic-sedimentary complexes were sampled at eight localities at the Taigonos Peninsula on the northern coast of the Sea of Okhotsk. Out of more than 250 samples, most proved to be completely remagnetized at the ﬁnal stage of deformation by the end of Early Cretaceous; this pervasive remagnetization is probably related to onset of volcanic activity in the Okhotsk–Chukotka belt. Geological data and overall agreement of these remagnetization directions with the Eurasian and North American reference values imply that the Taigonos Peninsula did not move with respect to the continental margin since the Early Cretaceous. A pre-remagnetization remanence was isolated only from Middle–Upper Jurassic cherts, where mean direction of a prefolding component ( D D 296º, I D 54º, a 95 D 4.5º; after tilt correction) was determined by combining four component directions and 20 remagnetization circles. These results imply the original position of the cherts at about 35ºN and their later northward transport over more than 3000 km. Geological data indicate docking of the studied chert units during the second half of the Early Cretaceous. Kinematic analysis shows that the only permissible scenario includes chert accumulation and subsequent motion on the Izanagi Plate and docking to the continental margin

We suspect that this region is among the least understood Phanero- zoic mobile belts worldwide, which is partly due to its vastness, difﬁcult access and natural conditions. Another reason is the extreme scarcity of paleo- magnetic data, in particular those satisfying the mod- ern quality standards. Recent studies [3,5] did reveal a strong late Mesozoic overprint in the rocks where ‘primary’ remanences had earlier been reported. The aim of this paper is to present paleomagnetic data from the Taigonos Peninsula along the northern coast of the Sea of Okhotsk (Fig. 1). This region is a segment of a long and narrow fold belt that separates early–middle Mesozoic structures to the north and west from the late Mesozoic–Cenozoic fold belt to the east and south. Thus determining the paleolati- tude of the Uda–Murgal fold belt and its segments impose strong constraints on the evolution of the structures situated between it and the Siberian plat- form. To avoid confusion, it will be referred to as the Uda–Murgal belt. Its southwestern part resides on the Siberian margin, whereas its central and eastern segments are surrounded by folded do- mains (Fig. 1). The belt comprises the remnants of late Paleozoic to Early Cretaceous island arcs which had probably marked the active Siberian margin [6]. In contrast, other units are suspected to have origi- nally been far away from this margin and accreted to it later [2]. Thus, this belt is clearly of a com- posite nature, and the original spatial and temporal relationship of its constituents is controversial. The Taigonos Peninsula on the northern coast of the Sea of Okhotsk is a part of the Uda–Murgal fold belt (Fig. 2). Received 1999 June 8; in original form 1998 October 22 SUMMARY Upper Jurassic red sandstones and red siltstones were collected from 67 layers at 12 localities in the Penglaizhen formation. This formation is in the north of Bazhong county (31.8°N, 106.7°E) in the Sichuan basin, which is located in the northern part of the Yangtze craton. Thermal demagnetization isolated a high-temperature magnetic component with a maximum unblocking temperature of about 690 °C from 45 layers. The primary nature of the magnetization acquisition is ascertained through the presence of magnetostratigraphic sequences with normal and reversed polarities, as well as positive fold and reversal tests at the 95 per cent conﬁdence level. assic palaeomagentic pole at 64.7°N, 236.0°E with A95=7.0° is calculated from the palaeo- magnetic directions of 11 localities. This pole position agrees with the two other Late Jurassic poles from the northern part of the Yangtze craton. A characteristic Late Jurassic pole is calculated from the three poles (68.6°N, 236.0°E with A95=8.0° ) for the northern part of the Yangtze craton. This pole position is signiﬁcantly diVerent from that for the southern part of the Yangtze craton. This suggests that the southern part of the Yangtze craton was subjected to southward extrusion by 1700 ± 1000 km with respect to the northern part. Intracraton deformation occurred within the Yangtze craton. Received 1999 June 15; in original form 1998 December 5 SUMMARY Recent interest has focused on whether South Korea may have undergone variable tectonic rotations since the Cretaceous. In an eVort to contribute to the answer to this question, we have completed a palaeomagnetic reconnaissance study of Early Cretaceous sedimentary and igneous rocks from the Kyongsang basin in southeast Korea. Stepwise thermal demagnetization isolated well-deﬁned characteristic magnetization in all samples. The palaeomagnetic directions reveal patterns of increasing amounts of clockwise (CW) rotation with increasing age for Aptian rock units. Palaeomagnetic declinations indicate clockwise vertical-axis rotations of R=34.3°± 6.9° for the early Aptian rock unit, R=24.9°± 10.6° for the middle Aptian, andR=−0.9°± 11.8° for the late Aptian relative to eastern Asia. The new Cretaceous palaeomagnetic data from this study are consistent with the hypothesis that Korea and other major parts of eastern Asia occupied the same relative positions in terms of palaeolatitudes in the Cretaceous.

A high- temperature magnetization component with unblocking temperatures of 670–690 °C was isolated from seven sites and yielded a positive fold test at the 95 per cent conﬁdence level. The high-temperature component is interpreted to be of primary origin because the folding age is Middle Triassic. The Pyeongan Supergroup is divided into four formations: the Hongjeom, Sadong, Gobangsan and Nogam formations in ascending order (Reedman & Um 1975; Lee 1987). The Nogam Formation is assigned an Early Triassic age on the basis of stratigraphic and structural data (Reedman & Um 1975). Conclusions Our paleomagnetic study of glaciomarine de- posits from the Sultanate of Oman was restricted in scope, yet the few results are likely to be unique for this area. It is virtually impossible to collect further sites from this study area. The number of outcrops with lithologies suitable for paleomag- netic studies is very limited. Moreover, the lithol- ogy changes rapidly both vertically and laterally so that most sampled sites could be traced later- ally for only a few meters. The samples contained two magnetic compo- nents. The low-temperature component is inter- preted to be a secondary magnetization related to the recent or modern geomagnetic ¢eld. The high-temperature component is interpreted as the characteristic remanent magnetization of probable primary origin. It yields a Late Precam- brian pole position for the Arabian peninsula at 31.6‡N 153.2‡E. The compatibility of this with other Gondwana poles may be regarded as evi- dence that the relative position of Arabia with respect to Africa 550 Ma ago was similar to the present con¢guration. The observed inclination of the characteristic remanent magnetization implies deposition of the glaciomarine Mirbat Sandstone Formation at a very low latitude ( V9.4‡). This result is compatible with other observations of shallow inclinations of magnetization in Late Pre- cambrian glaciogenic deposits. Acknowledgements We are grateful to Mohammed Kassim a

Introduction Our understanding of the tectonic evolution of China since the Permian has been greatly im- proved thanks to intensive geological and paleo- magnetic investigations in the last two decades. However, the picture for pre-Permian time is less clear. Paleomagnetic experience indicates that the older the rocks, the more di⁄cult they are to work with. This is because older rocks ex- perience longer and usually more complicated geological history, and their original magnetiza- tion is thus often modi¢ed by later geomagnetic events and sometimes completely obliterated. The Leijiatun Fm is 87 m thick, and consists of yellowish green shales with subordinate bioclastic and nodular limestones. Introduction Our understanding of the tectonic evolution of China since the Permian has been greatly im- proved thanks to intensive geological and paleo- magnetic investigations in the last two decades. However, the picture for pre-Permian time is less clear. Paleomagnetic experience indicates that the older the rocks, the more di⁄cult they are to work with. This is because older rocks ex- perience longer and usually more complicated geological history, and their original magnetiza- tion is thus often modi¢ed by later geomagnetic events and sometimes completely obliterated. For this reason, it should not come as a surprise that paleomagnetic results reported from the Paleozoic or older rocks from each of the major tectonic blocks in China are much fewer than those from younger rocks. The Silurian sequence near Shiqian is repre- sented by the Leijiatun section about 5 km north of downtown Shiqian. The lithology and fossil record of this section are correlative with the Rongxi section in southern Sichuan [8]. The Low- er Silurian Series includes, in ascending order, the Longmaxi, Xiangshuyuan, Leijiatun and Majiao- chong formations. The Longmaxi Fm at this sec- tion is only 6 m thick, consisting of gray shales, disconformably overlying limestones of the Upper Ordovician Guanyinqiao Fm, and yielding abun- dant graptolites. The Xiangshuyuan Fm is 68 m in thickness, the lower part of which is composed of yellowish green shales interbedded with lime- stones and bioclastic limestones, and the upper part of which is composed of gray thick-bedded bioclastic limestones. The Leijiatun Fm is 87 m thick, and consists of yellowish green shales with subordinate bioclastic and nodular limestones. Both the Xiangshuyuan and Leijiatun formations are rich in coral, conodont and brachiopod fos- sils. The Majiaochong Fm is 60 m in thickness and is composed primarily of yellowish green shales. This paper presents paleomagnetic results from the Paleoproterozoic Uaua mafic dykes, situated in the northeastern part of the SBo Francisco Craton, Brazil (Fig. 2). A comparison with the Paleoproterozoic poles from the Kalahari Craton is presented and a tectonic model is proposed. The UMC consists of quartz-feldspathic banded gneisses, tonalitic to granodioritic ortho-gneisses, migmatites, amphibolites, ultramafic and supracrustal rocks, partially rejuvenated during the Transamazonian cycle (2.2-1.8 Ga) (Beurlen, 1970; Winge and Danni, 1980; Bastos Leal, 1992). The area which encloses the Uaua dykes shows a sigmoidal geometric pattern outlined and limited by shear zones which affect both the rocks of the UMC and the dykes (Bastos Lea1 et al. 1994). Two groups of mafic dykes are recognized, based on field and petrographic data (Bellieni et al., 1995): The first group (metamorphic dykes-MD) is composed of amphibolites with fine-grained homogeneous texture with a distinct schistosity developed before the Transamazonian cycle (Jardim de Sa et al., 1984). These dykes trend N-S and have a maximum thick- ness of 2m. Several amphibole K-Ar ages (MD dykes) between 2. Well-dated Paleoproterozoic paleomagnetic poles from the West African and north Amazonian cratons led Onstott and Dorbor (1987) and Renne et al. (1988) to suggest a movement of these two cratons relative to the Kalahari Craton during this time. For the intervening Sao Francisco/Congo Craton in western Gondwana (Fig. l), however, few Paleoproterozoic paleomagnetic poles have been available. Paleomagnetic studies of Paleoproterozoic units from the Sao Francisco/Congo craton would be important to elucidate the paleogeographic evolution of the western Gondwana cratons at this time. This paper presents paleomagnetic results from the Paleoproterozoic Uaua mafic dykes, situated in the northeastern part of the SBo Francisco Craton, Brazil (Fig. 2). A comparison with the Paleoproterozoic poles from the Kalahari Craton is presented and a tectonic model is proposed. In this study, paleomagnetic results from Cretaceous rocks in the Eumsung basin are presented by comparing the results with those from the Gyeongsang basin and other Cre- taceous basins in order to clarify the magnetic and tectonic characteristics of the basin. In terms of the age of granites in the study area, Cheong et al. (1976) suggested that the granite in the eastern part of the basin is Jurassic in age, and that of the granite in the west is Cretaceous. However, Chun et al. (1994) recently argued that the granite in the west to the basin formed in Jurassic. A paleomagnetic investigation of the granites in the Eumsung basin is carried out to constrain the age of the granites utiliz- ing the timing of the magnetization of the granites. 2. Geologic Setting The Eumsung basin is a pull-apart basin formed between left-stepping sinistral “master” strike slip faults, and ﬁlled with Cretaceous sedimentary rocks which were named as the Chopyeong Formation (Chun et al., 1994). Precambrian gneiss and Jurassic granite comprise the basement of the basin and volcanic rocks are distributed along the eastern boundary of the basin (Lee and Kim, 1971; Cheong et al., 337 338 S.-J. southeastern part of the Korea Peninsula. Cretaceous basins in South Korea can be sorted into three groups by their areal distributions. The Gyeongsang basin is composed of three sub-basins and occupies the largest area compared to other Cretaceous basins. The second one comprises small-sized basins, compared to the Gyeongsang basin, and is distributed along the Ogcheon Belt. The third group consists of basins located in the Kyeonggi massif parallel to the boundary of the Ogcheon Belt. In the laboratory, samples were cut into 2.2 cm long cylin- ders. Remanent magnetization of specimens was measured using a Molspin spinner magnetometer. In this chapter, the rock magnetic properties of sediments will be summarized briefly with respect to their mineralogy, particulary of red beds and types of remanence. Although no specific rock magnetic studies have been carried out, a general overview is thought to be relevant for the results obtained. For a more extensive discussion of palaeomagnetism and rock magnetism, see Nagata (1961), Irving (1964), Stacey and Banerjee (L974) and McElhinny (1973). The main points are summarized below. 1. In sedimentary rocks, haematite is one of the most stable magnetic phase under oxidising conditions (O’Reilly, 1976) and can be of both syn- and post-depositional origin in red beds. Other types of sedimentary rocks such as varved clays may more directly reflect mineralogy related to the source material in the bed rock terrain and can be expected to contain both haematite and magnetite as detrital minerals. 2. Considerable emphasis was therefore placed on the study of igneous rocks and in particular on the early Tertiary Deccan Traps and the Early Cretaceous Rajmahal Traps (see review of Klootwijk, 1979a). These early palaeomagnetic studies were then extended to sedimentary successions, mainly red beds intercalated in the more basal part of the Gondwana System. In this chapter, the rock magnetic properties of sediments will be summarized briefly with respect to their mineralogy, particulary of red beds and types of remanence. Although no specific rock magnetic studies have been carried out, a general overview is thought to be relevant for the results obtained. For a more extensive discussion of palaeomagnetism and rock magnetism, see Nagata (1961), Irving (1964), Stacey and Banerjee (L974) and McElhinny (1973). The main points are summarized below. 1. In sedimentary rocks, haematite is one of the most stable magnetic phase under oxidising conditions (O’Reilly, 1976) and can be of both syn- and post-depositional origin in red beds. Other types of sedimentary rocks such as varved clays may more directly reflect mineralogy related to the source material in the bed rock terrain and can be expected to contain both haematite and magnetite as detrital minerals. 2. The total Natural Remanent Magnetization (NRM) of rocks is commonly a vector sum of several different types of remanent magnetization. In sedimentary rocks, haematite is one of the most stable magnetic phase under oxidising conditions (O’Reilly, 1976) and can be of both syn- and post-depositional origin in red beds. Other types of sedimentary rocks such as varved clays may more directly reflect mineralogy related to the source material in the bed rock terrain and can be expected to contain both haematite and magnetite as detrital minerals. 2. The total Natural Remanent Magnetization (NRM) of rocks is commonly a vector sum of several different types of remanent magnetization. The magnetization may be acquired at the time of formation of the rock or at a later stage. In sedimentary rocks possible types of remanence are a.) The palaeomagnetic results from Permo-Carboniferous to late-Early Permian rocks are open to two interpretations - Primary or Secondary of Triassic-Jurassic age. For primary interpretation the results are seemingly in disagreement with some earlier established results and invoke an appreciable polar wandering during Permian time. An alternative explanation in terms of a Triassic-Jurassic remagnetization may be invoked because of their similarity with the Triassic-Jurassic trajectory in the Indo-Pakistan APWP as proposed before. This interpretation however, seems less likely because of the predominantly reversed polarities of the results obtained, compared with the world-wide normal polarity bias which has been established for the Triassic-Jurassic. The Permo-Triassic and middle to Late Triassic results are in gross agreement with established results of the Indo-Pakistan and add further support for the existence of a Triassic-Jurassic loop in the APWP. The sections sampled for magnetic polarity rever- sal studies are located at the eastern side of the southeastern Pyrenean fore- land basin (Figs. 1B and 2). The sedimentary rocks that crop out in this area are Paleocene to Oligocene in age and consist of continental deposits that are below and above marine strata. These marine sediments are traditionally considered to be middle to upper Eocene in age (e.g., Hottinger, 1960; Ferrer, 1967, 1971; Reguant, 1967; Via, 1969; Serra-Kiel, 1984). The sedi- mentary formations distinguished by several authors among the marine Eocene deposits of the Vic sector of the southeastern Pyrenean foreland basin are shown schematically (Fig. 3) after the synthesis proposed in Taberner (1983). The base of the marine sequence has been interpreted as marking a rapid late Lutetian to Bartonian transgression that occurred as a result of the emplacement of the floor thrust of the Pyrenean antiformal stack (Puigdefàbregas et al., 1986). East of Vic, the basal marine strata have been dated as middle Lutetian age (Serra-Kiel, 1984). However, the first marine deposits in the southern sector of the basin were interpreted as lower-mid

diachronous and to span from middle Lutet- ian time to the base of chron C18r at 41.2 Ma (Bartonian). The top of the marine section was considered to be lower Priabonian age based on (1) nummulite species present beneath the youngest reef deposits (Serra-Kiel, 1984) and (2) the micromammal assemblage and charophyte biozonation in the continental sediments above the marine interval, that sug- gest an upper Eocene–Oligocene age (Agustí et al., 1987; Anadon et al., 1987; Feist et al., 1994). Burbank et al. (1992a) linked the top of their mag- netostratigraphic section from the Vic sector of the basin and the evaporites equivalent to the Cardona Formation to the significant sea-level fall that oc- curred at the Bartonian-Priabonian boundary (Haq et al., 1987), and gave an age of around 40 Ma for the evaporites of the Cardona Formation (located in Fig. 3). However, Vergés and Burbank (1996) and Serra-Kiel et al. (1998) linked these evaporites to the base of the Priabonian (37.2 Ma) after reeval- uation of the original magnetostratigraphic data (Burbank et al., 1992a) against the revised GPTS produced by Cande and Kent (1995). The sections sampled for magnetic polarity rever- sal studies are located at the eastern side of the southeastern Pyrenean fore- land basin (Figs. 1B and 2). The sedimentary rocks that crop out in this area are Paleocene to Oligocene in age and consist of continental deposits that are below and above marine strata. These marine sediments are traditionally considered to be middle to upper Eocene in age (e.g., Hottinger, 1960; Ferrer, 1967, 1971; Reguant, 1967; Via, 1969; Serra-Kiel, 1984). The sedi- mentary formations distinguished by several authors among the marine Eocene deposits of the Vic sector of the southeastern Pyrenean foreland basin are shown schematically (Fig. 3) after the synthesis proposed in Taberner (1983). The base of the marine sequence has been interpreted as marking a rapid late Lutetian to Bartonian transgression that occurred as a result of the emplacement of the floor thrust of the Pyrenean antiformal stack (Puigdefàbregas et al., 1986). East of Vic, the basal marine strata have been dated as middle Lutetian age (Serra-Kiel, 1984). However, the first marine deposits in the southern sector of the basin were interpreted as lower-mid

diachronous and to span from middle Lutet- ian time to the base of chron C18r at 41.2 Ma (Bartonian). The top of the marine section was considered to be lower Priabonian age based on (1) nummulite species present beneath the youngest reef deposits (Serra-Kiel, 1984) and (2) the micromammal assemblage and charophyte biozonation in the continental sediments above the marine interval, that sug- gest an upper Eocene–Oligocene age (Agustí et al., 1987; Anadon et al., 1987; Feist et al., 1994). Burbank et al. (1992a) linked the top of their mag- netostratigraphic section from the Vic sector of the basin and the evaporites equivalent to the Cardona Formation to the significant sea-level fall that oc- curred at the Bartonian-Priabonian boundary (Haq et al., 1987), and gave an age of around 40 Ma for the evaporites of the Cardona Formation (located in Fig. 3). However, Vergés and Burbank (1996) and Serra-Kiel et al. (1998) linked these evaporites to the base of the Priabonian (37.2 Ma) after reeval- uation of the original magnetostratigraphic data (Burbank et al., 1992a) against the revised GPTS produced by Cande and Kent (1995). The sedimentary rocks that crop out in this area are Paleocene to Oligocene in age and consist of continental deposits that are below and above marine strata. These marine sediments are traditionally considered to be middle to upper Eocene in age (e.g., Hottinger, 1960; Ferrer, 1967, 1971; Reguant, 1967; Via, 1969; Serra-Kiel, 1984). The sedi- mentary formations distinguished by several authors among the marine Eocene deposits of the Vic sector of the southeastern Pyrenean foreland basin are shown schematically (Fig. 3) after the synthesis proposed in Taberner (1983). The base of the marine sequence has been interpreted as marking a rapid late Lutetian to Bartonian transgression that occurred as a result of the emplacement of the floor thrust of the Pyrenean antiformal stack (Puigdefàbregas et al., 1986). East of Vic, the basal marine strata have been dated as middle Lutetian age (Serra-Kiel, 1984). However, the first marine deposits in the southern sector of the basin were interpreted as lower-mid

diachronous and to span from middle Lutet- ian time to the base of chron C18r at 41.2 Ma (Bartonian). The top of the marine section was considered to be lower Priabonian age based on (1) nummulite species present beneath the youngest reef deposits (Serra-Kiel, 1984) and (2) the micromammal assemblage and charophyte biozonation in the continental sediments above the marine interval, that sug- gest an upper Eocene–Oligocene age (Agustí et al., 1987; Anadon et al., 1987; Feist et al., 1994). Burbank et al. However, Vergés and Burbank (1996) and Serra-Kiel et al. These events include development of the San Andreas–San Jacinto fault system and uplift of the Transverse Ranges. The badlands sequence also spans three of the four most recent North American Land Mammal “ages” and therefore coincides with important trans-Beringian and Neotropical mammal dispersal events. At BGC, only thermal demagnetization techniques were performed. After measuring the intensity and direction of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of all samples, each was subsequently demagnetized by stepwise heating at 40 °C intervals starting at 120 and ending at 680 °C. In order to determine the dominant magnetic mineral, Hehn et al. (1996) subjected 15 samples from the Eden Hot Springs–Jack Rabbit Trail section to isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) analysis. Of these, 13 showed sat- uration magnetization behavior indicative of magnetite as the dominant car- rier, whereas two samples showed behavior suggestive of hematite. Behavior during thermal demagnetization showed the removal of a low-temperature overprint component, possibly due to goethite, by 200 °C. At successively higher temperatures, consistent magnetization directions were generally ob- tained to about 560 °C, above which decreases in intensity and unpredictable changes in direction occurred. This supports the conclusion that magnetite was the primary carrier of the characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM), given a Curie temperature for that mineral of about 580 °C. This paper details the development of that framework by using paleo- magnetic and mammalian biochronological data. It modifies and expands upon the magnetostratigraphic foundation developed in Hehn et al. (1996) for the lower part of the Badlands section and presents new mag- neto-biostratigraphic data for the upper part. The new framework is then used to reexamine, and refine where necessary, the timing of local tec- tonic and sedimentological events recorded within the sequence. There are 22 major reversal boundaries in the global magnetic polarity time scale (MPTS) over the ~6 m.y. represented by the Badlands sequence, thus allowing a potential geologic resolution at a scale of about 0.27 m.y. This paper also reexamines the counterclockwise tectonic rotation of the Badlands region reported in Hehn et al. (1996). It briefly attempts to resolve the discrepancy between the paleomagnetic data and previous models based on seismic studies that predict clockwise vertical axis rotation in this region. Also presented are new age estimates for fossil mammal-bearing localities collected in the Badlands during the early part of the twentieth century, such as the Mount Eden and El Casco local fau

one that is not statistically significant, but in which the polarity determination is not in doubt; i. e., usually a site in which two of three samples “have nearly parallel magnetic vectors with the third being divergent” (Johnson et al., 1982, p. 21). This can also include a site where one sample was lost or dam- aged but the remaining two have concordant directions. Class III sites were those having all three vectors widely divergent; these were rejected from the database. A class IV site is one in which only a single sample is available for analysis (as in Hehn et al., 1996). Class IV sites cannot be used alone for de- termination of the polarity of a particular section, but can corroborate po- larity data from class I sites, thereby contributing qualitatively to the level of confidence with which one assigns the polarity of that section. Of 198 sampled sites, four were lost, five were rejected on the basis of tenuous stratigraphic or structural associations, and six were rejected on the basis of class III status leaving 183 accepted sites. Of these, 141 were des- ignated class I, 31 as class II, and 11 as class IV . Apart from this behavior, the path of the demagnetization vector in sites SI40-SI42 is relatively simple. All specimens converge linearly on the origin of the Zijderveld plot at demagnetization temperatures above 500øC. The Curie point is less than 570øC, and sometimes less than 550øC, suggesting that a titanomagnetite, with a varying proportion of Ti, is the dominant magnetic carrier. The primary magnetization has been entirely replaced in these two sites, perhaps by weathering or lightning-induced components. 4.2.4. Interpretation. Stable characteristic magnetizations could be isolated from 13 sites in the Malue Beds and three sites in the Mbo Lavas (Table 1). With the exception of sites SI53 and SI54, which appear to record a short interval of normal polarity and an intermediate polarity transition, the characteristic

om sites SI31-SI39, at the top of the sequence, all have H c _< 5 mT; specimens from the rest of the sequence have H c > 5 mT. Overprinting in specimens from sites SI31-SI39 is associated with a decrease in H c. Lower coercivity may have made these specimens more susceptible to remagnetization by viscous remanent magnetization (VRM), which would be expected to have a direction close to the dipole field direction (if it has been accumulated over a long timescale). However, the high AF fields needed to remove this component are inconsistent with VRM. Alternatively, the overprint may be a chemical remanence, acquired by the growth of magnetite after the beds were tilted, possibly by the oxidation of iron sulfides during weathering. Similarly intense and stable overprinting (often interpreted, rightly or wrongly, as a VRM) has frequently been reported from carbonates and silts in carbonate associations [e.g., Creer, 1959; Achache et al., 1982; Scotese et al., 1982]. 4.2.3. stimated as the angular standard deviation of the VGP distribution 14.9 ø +6.50/-3.5 ø, is close to expected, suggesting that the paleomagnetic pole represents a time-averaged field. Moreover, five new 4øAr/39Ar plateau ages, falling between 9.20 and 13.55 Ma, were obtained. Thellier paleointensity experiments were carried out on both basalts and baked sediments. Almost all basalts are chemically unstable during the laboratory heatings and of the 36 preselected samples only three yield usable results. In contrast, the baked sediments are ideal for Thellier experiments with 11 out of 13 samples giving reliable paleointensity estimates. Rock magnetic experiments show that the main ferromagnetic minerals in the baked sediments are fine-grained magnetite and hematite with a large proportion of superparamagnetic grains. In addition to the standard partial thermoremanent magnetization (pTRM) check, used in Thellier experiments to detect chemical/crystalline alteration, we introduce a second \"pTRM tail\" check designed to test the basic prerequisite of the method, namely, the equality of unblocking and blocking temperatures. For the baked sediments, unblocking and blocking temperatures are found to be identical, which indicates that the remanence is carried by single-domain grains. 1

Methods and Results consistent normal-polarity overprint component was often removed during AF and thermal demagnetization below 30 mT and 250øC (Figure 3b) and is most apparent in specimens with reversed-polarity characteristic magnetizations (Figures 3d, 3e, and 3f). At some sites, specimens contain both normal- and reversed-polarity characteristic magnetizations (Table 1). At several other sites the data are also indicative of a second component of magnetization at the high end of the demagneti- zation curve, but the signal is too noisy to be fitted with either least squares lines or planes. The thermal and AF demagnetization data are consistent with magnetite being the remanence-carrying magnetic min- eral in most of these rocks. In samples from ~10 to 20% of the sites, however, the demagnetization data indicate that hematite with blocking temperatures >600øC, apparently in varying amounts, is also present in these samples. In most cases, there is no difference in the characteristic direction of magnetization between the two mineral phases within a given specimen (Figure 3e), but in some cases, magnetite appears to carry a component of one polarity and hematite appears to carry a second, higher-temperature component of the opposite polarity. The remanent magnetization of individual specimens, cut from the core samples, was measured with a cryogenic magnetometer. Specimens from all samples were progressively demagnetized with standard alternating field (AF) and thermal procedures to peak inductions of 100 mT and maximum temperatures of 675øC, respectively. Hagstrum U.S. Geological Survey, Menlo Park, California Donald A. Swanson U.S. Geological Survey, Hawaiian Volcano Observatory, Hawaii National Park Russell C. Evarts U.S. Geological Survey, Menlo Park, California Abstract. Paleomagnetic data from a transect across the Cascade arc in southern Washington were collected to test models of vertical axis rotations for this part of the Pacific Northwest and to provide information on the tectonic history of the St. Helens seismic zone. The 75 site-mean directions are divided into three groups based on isotopic, fission track, and stratigraphic ages. Group 1 consists of samples from rocks deposited between 39 and 30 Ma and shows a mean clockwise vertical axis rotation of 34 ø + 13 ø, group 2 consists of samples from rocks deposited be- tween 30 and 24 Ma and shows a mean clockwise rotation of 17 ø + 11 o, and group 3 consists of samples from rocks between 24 and 16 Ma and shows a mean clockwise rotation of 20 ø + 12 ø. Al- though these three values of rotation are statistically indistinguishable at the 95% confid

eismic zone (SHZ). The available paleomagnetic data for Eocene-Oligocene rocks west of the seismic zone show clockwise vertical axis rotations of 30 ø + 8 ø and 35 ø + 9 ø consistent with the value for group 1. The rotational values for groups 2 and 3 and the intrusive suite of Kidd Creek (13 Ma), despite their different ages, have similar values east of the SHZ. Comparing these groups of data east and west of the seismic zone indicates a differential rotation of 10 ø + 3 ø across it. In addition, the rates of rotation in southern Washington are similar to those for rocks in the western Cascades of Oregon and indicate that rotational deformation of Miocene age extends northward into southern Washington and eastward into the axis of the arc. 1. At some sites, specimens contain both normal- and reversed-polarity characteristic magnetizations (Table 1). At several other sites the data are also indicative of a second component of magnetization at the high end of the demagneti- zation curve, but the signal is too noisy to be fitted with either least squares lines or planes. The thermal and AF demagnetization data are consistent with magnetite being the remanence-carrying magnetic min- eral in most of these rocks. In samples from ~10 to 20% of the sites, however, the demagnetization data indicate that hematite with blocking temperatures >600øC, apparently in varying amounts, is also present in these samples. In most cases, there is no difference in the characteristic direction of magnetization between the two mineral phases within a given specimen (Figure 3e), but in some cases, magnetite appears to carry a component of one polarity and hematite appears to carry a second, higher-temperature component of the opposite polarity. Paleomagnetic data from a transect across the Cascade arc in southern Washington were collected to test models of vertical axis rotations for this part of the Pacific Northwest and to provide information on the tectonic history of the St. Helens seismic zone. The 75 site-mean directions are divided into three groups based on isotopic, fission track, and stratigraphic ages. Group 1 consists of samples from rocks deposited between 39 and 30 Ma and shows a mean clockwise vertical axis rotation of 34 ø + 13 ø, group 2 consists of samples from rocks deposited be- tween 30 and 24 Ma and shows a mean clockwise rotation of 17 ø + 11 o, and group 3 consists of samples from rocks between 24 and 16 Ma and shows a mean clockwise rotation of 20 ø + 12 ø. The available paleomagnetic data for Eocene-Oligocene rocks west of the seismic zone show clockwise vertical axis rotations of 30 ø + 8 ø and 35 ø + 9 ø consistent with the value for group 1. The rotational values for groups 2 and 3 and the intrusive suite of Kidd Creek (13 Ma), despite their different ages, have similar values east of the SHZ. Comparing these groups of data east and west of the seismic zone indicates a differential rotation of 10 ø + 3 ø across it. At several other sites the data are also indicative of a second component of magnetization at the high end of the demagneti- zation curve, but the signal is too noisy to be fitted with either least squares lines or planes. The origin of the curvature of the Median Tectonic Line (MTL) in southwest Japan is still controversial. In order to investigate its formation, we carried out a paleomagnetic study in the Nohi area, north of the curved part of the MTL in the eastern part of southwest Japan. More than 420 paleomagnetic samples were collected at 35 sites from Cretaceous to Paleogene welded tuffs in the Kasagatake Rhyolites, Oamamiyama Group, and Nohi Rhyolite. Characteristic directions with high unblocking temperature component above 560øC were isolated from 32 sites. Paleomagnetic directions of the Kasagatake Rhyolites and Oamamiyama Group (55-66 Ma) have a clockwise deflected declination (D = 51.7 ø, I = 52.6 ø, oz95 = 8.6 ø) which is consistent with the characteristic Paleogene paleomagnetic direction of the central part of southwest Japan. A similarly deflected declination is also observed in the peripheral part of the Nohi Rhyolite region, far away from the Atera fault system. Paleomagnetic data indicate that the Nohi area experienced a clockwise rotation through more than 45 ø with respect to the Asian continent as a part of southwest Japan

[1975] estimated unblocking temperatures at about 250øC (350øC) for single-domain magnetite (hematite) grains which acquired vis- cous partial thermoremanent magnetization in the last 1 Ma. It may be possible that the welded tuffs along the fault suffered complete remagnetization during the fault activity of the Atera fault system in the last 2 Ma and later acquired viscous partial thermoremanent magnetization. The remagnetization may have occurred presumably due to fluid migration within a short duration of one reversed polarity period. This mechanism can explain three observations: (1) only reversed polarity, (2) non- deflected direction from the south, and (3) small dispersion in declination. Much work still is needed

The Late Cretaceous to Paleogene igneous activity is divided into five stages, I to V in ascending stratigraphic order [Harayama et al., 1985]. The origin of the curvature of the Median Tectonic Line (MTL) in southwest Japan is still controversial. In order to investigate its formation, we carried out a paleomagnetic study in the Nohi area, north of the curved part of the MTL in the eastern part of southwest Japan. More than 420 paleomagnetic samples were collected at 35 sites from Cretaceous to Paleogene welded tuffs in the Kasagatake Rhyolites, Oamamiyama Group, and Nohi Rhyolite. Characteristic directions with high unblocking temperature component above 560øC were isolated from 32 sites. Paleomagnetic directions of the Kasagatake Rhyolites and Oamamiyama Group (55-66 Ma) have a clockwise deflected declination (D = 51.7 ø, I = 52.6 ø, oz95 = 8.6 ø) which is consistent with the characteristic Paleogene paleomagnetic direction of the central part of southwest Japan. A similarly deflected declination is also observed in the peripheral part of the Nohi Rhyolite region, far away from the Atera fault system. Paleomagnetic data indicate that the Nohi area experienced a clockwise rotation through more than 45 ø with respect to the Asian continent as a part of southwest Japan

The origin of the curvature of the Median Tectonic Line (MTL) in southwest Japan is still controversial. In order to investigate its formation, we carried out a paleomagnetic study in the Nohi area, north of the curved part of the MTL in the eastern part of southwest Japan. More than 420 paleomagnetic samples were collected at 35 sites from Cretaceous to Paleogene welded tuffs in the Kasagatake Rhyolites, Oamamiyama Group, and Nohi Rhyolite. Characteristic directions with high unblocking temperature component above 560øC were isolated from 32 sites. Paleomagnetic directions of the Kasagatake Rhyolites and Oamamiyama Group (55-66 Ma) have a clockwise deflected declination (D = 51.7 ø, I = 52.6 ø, oz95 = 8.6 ø) which is consistent with the characteristic Paleogene paleomagnet

a indicate that the Nohi area experienced a clockwise rotation through more than 45 ø with respect to the Asian continent as a part of southwest Japan but that the amount of rotation of the Nohi area is 23 ø smaller than that of the central part of southwest Japan. A new model is developed to explain the tectonic rotation. At about 15 Ma during the latest stage of the clockwise rotation of southwest Japan, the eastern end moved southward by more than 60 km along a left-lateral strike-slip fault which comprised the present north-south segment of the MTL and the Akaishi Tectonic Line. We conclude that the curvature of the MTL is a composite of the 15 Ma strike-slip fault system and a small bend of the MTL associated with the small differential rotation of the Nohi area with respect to the central part of southwest Japan. 1. Later paleomagnetic studies established that SW Japan experienced clockwise rota- tion in Miocene times [e.g., Otofuji, 1996]: More than 40 ø of rotation is claimed and the climax of rotation is dated to 15 Ma. of SW Japan. The curvature of the Median Tectonic Line (MTL) is a clue to the higher-order approximation of the tectonics for SW Japan (Figure 1). Analysis of Paleomagnetic Results The analysis of the paleomagnetic data illus- trates well the difficulties in obtaining reliable re- sults from shallow-water carbonates and diamic- tites. Remanence directions from the carbonates of the Trezona and Nuccaleena Formations are widely scattered and poorly defined. Their rela- tively low unblocking temperatures (<600 °C) and isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) tests of the magnetic mineralogy in these forma- tions (method of Lowrie, 1990) suggest that mag- netite and goethite are the principal remanence carriers. The scattering and poor definition of the magnetization directions, as well as the common presence of goethite, suggest that the carbonates carry unstable magnetizations unsuitable for use in paleomagnetic studies. Thus, the carbonates have not been included in subsequent analysis. The Yaltipena and Elatina Formations yielded much better results overall. Two components of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) could be consistently iden

d during the Ter- tiary uplift of the Flinders Ranges (Wellman and Greenhalgh, 1988). In both the Yaltipena and Elatina samples, the site mean C component directions have moder- ate to shallow inclinations and either north- northwest or southwest declinations (Fig. 6), al- though there are slight differences in the distribution of the site mean directions from section to section (see Table 1 for summary of data). The overall remanence direction for the Elatina Formation in this study (site mean D = 212.1°, I = –16.9° for 58 sites) is similar to those directions previously published (e.g., D = 197.4°, I = –7.1° for 10 sites; Schmidt and Williams, 1995). In contrast to the A and C components, the B component is not well defined (Fig. 5, B and D); on the site level, the remanence directions are spread out in a broad band with generally north- west directions. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S,

(corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S, 304.8° E, A95=8.3° ; U–Pb age of 2436± 25 Ma), the Voche-Lambina ultramaﬁcs and amphibolites (12.9 ° N, 314.1° E, A95=8.6° ; Rb–Sr age of 2198 ± 172 Ma), and the Kolvitsa peridotites and schists (44.2° N, 232.6° E, A95=5.4° ; assigned magnetization age of 1900 Ma). For the Karelian Province, reference poles are presented for the Burakovka gabbro-norites (19.5 ° S, 262.6° E, A95=7.2° ; Sm–Nd age of 2439± 22 Ma), the Matozero doleritic dykes (20.6° S, 308.5° E, A95=12.3° ; U–Pb age of 2150 ± 60 Ma), and the Ropruchey Sill gabbro- dolerites (40.5 ° N, 229.8° E, A95=8.1° ; U–Pb age of 1770 ± 12 Ma). Although some NRM components of other rocks are not as precisely dated, a number of palaeomagnetic poles are in good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP). A preliminary version of the pre-Svecofennian APWP tracks for the Karelian and Kola–Belomorian provinces is proposed. Our results conﬁrm the general drift pattern of Fennoscandia in the Proterozoic and support the idea of the absence of large-scale block movements within t

gnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction of the Fennoscandian APWP. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). n good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP). A preliminary version of the pre-Svecofennian APWP tracks for the Karelian and Kola–Belomorian provinces is proposed. Our results conﬁrm the general drift pattern of Fennoscandia in the Proterozoic and support the idea of the absence of large-scale block movements within the Fennoscandian Shield since Jatulian times (2300–2100 Ma). To help constrain the relative positions of the various tectonic blocks of the eastern Fennoscandian Shield during pre-Jatulian times, more new palaeomagnetic and radiometric data need to be added to the available palaeomagnetic database. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S,

gnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction of the Fennoscandian APWP. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction of the Fennoscandian APWP. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Rock Magnetic Properties Before proceeding to paleointensity measurements we have scrutinized several rock magnetic parameters. The viscosity index (v)of 235 specimens has been calculated by using a modification of the original Thellier method [Thellier and Thellier, 1944] in which the z axes of the specimens were oriented parallel and then antiparallel to the direction of the ambiant magnetic field (40 gT)for 10 days, respectively. The stable NRM is then calculated as half the sum and the viscous remanent magnetization (VRM) as half the difference of the total remanences measured after each cycle. Seventy-seven percent of the specimens are characterized by a v value (v = VRM/NRM x 100) lower than 6%. Seven flows from the ME section have v as high as 40%. No paleointensity determination was obtained in these cases (if we remove these flows, the mean value of v is 4.5). Eighty-five percent of the specimens have a viscosity lower than 10 with a mean value of 2.5. GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND SAMPLING DETAILS The western third of Madagascar comprises an ex- tensive sequence of gently west dipping Phanerozoic sedimentary rocks within three basins, referred to from north to south as the Diego, Majunga and Moron- dava Basins (Fig. 1). The Sakoa Group, the oldest rocks in the Morondava Basin, consist of Late Carboni- ferous-Early Permian tillites, overlain by Early Permian coal-bearing horizons and redbeds, and Middle Per- mian marine limestones (Fig. 2). The Sakoa Group of the Morondava Basin is most commonly referred to as Late Carboniferous-Mid Permian in age (Besairie and Collignon, 19721, but Hankel (1994) places the basal Sakoa Group within the Early Permian (Asselian). The Sakamena Group, which unconformably over- lies the Sakoa Group, comprises Late Permian con- tinental sandstones and conglomerates, followed by Early Triassic alternating continental sandstones and marine shales. GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND SAMPLING DETAILS The western third of Madagascar comprises an ex- tensive sequence of gently west dipping Phanerozoic sedimentary rocks within three basins, referred to from north to south as the Diego, Majunga and Moron- dava Basins (Fig. 1). The Sakoa Group, the oldest rocks in the Morondava Basin, consist of Late Carboni- ferous-Early Permian tillites, overlain by Early Permian coal-bearing horizons and redbeds, and Middle Per- mian marine limestones (Fig. 2). The Sakoa Group of the Morondava Basin is most commonly referred to as Late Carboniferous-Mid Permian in age (Besairie and Collignon, 19721, but Hankel (1994) places the basal Sakoa Group within the Early Permian (Asselian). The Sakamena Group, which unconformably over- lies the Sakoa Group, comprises Late Permian con- tinental sandstones and conglomerates, followed by Early Triassic alternating continental sandstones and marine shales. Interestingly, the transitional or anomalous virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) tend to cluster in two nearly antipodal regions, one in the northern Pacific Ocean and the other in the southwest Indian Ocean. Magnetic characteristics The demagnetization results reveal fairly simple magnetization behavior as would be expected for young volcanic rocks. In general, only one or two components of magnetization are present, with the low-to-medium unblocking temperature and low coercivity component being either a small present-day overprint or an overprint related to lightning strikes (Fig. 3). These overprint direc- tions were easily removed in all but a few samples by demagnetization up to 30 mT or 480‡C. The remaining magnetization is interpreted as the characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) acquired as the volcanic rocks cooled shortly after extrusion. The ChRM is likely carried by pseudo- single domain titanium-poor titanomagnetite or magnetite, as evidenced by hysteresis results and the rapid decay of the majority of the magnetiza- tion between 500‡C and 580‡C during thermal de- magnetization. In general, AF demagnetization results are less noisy than thermal demagnetiza- tion, though both methods resolve the ChRM well and give similar mean directions. For exam- ple, the mean direction computed from all sites using only thermally demagnetized samples di¡ers from the mean using only AF-demagnetized sam- ples by less than 0.8‡. Thus, propagation and localization in central Afar have not had the same influence in causing crustal block rotations or, perhaps more likely, have not reached the same stage of evolution as seen in eastern Afar. In addition, several of the lava flows record intriguing geomagnetic field behavior associated with polarity transitions, excursions, or large secular variation events. Interestingly, the transitional or anomalous virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) tend to cluster in two nearly antipodal regions, one in the northern Pacific Ocean and the other in the southwest Indian Ocean. One lava flow has recorded both of the antipodal transitional components, with the two components residing in magnetic minerals with unblocking temperatures above and below V500‡C, respectively. In eastern Afar, this situation has evolved to localized extension associated with the westward propagation of the Gulf of Aden/Gulf of Tadjurah seafloor spreading system into the Asal^Ghoubbet Rift. End-member models are either autochthonous, requiring in situ Phanerozoic reworking of the pre-Cambrian crust, or allochthonous, including accretion of mobile Caledonian and Variscan terranes. Continent-scale Variscan right-lateral displacements along the TESZ have been also postulated. A paleomagnetic study of Upper Silurian diabases from the southern part of Holy Cross Mts. (central Poland) was undertaken to test between these models. A primary characteristic magnetization was isolated in these rocks. It passes the fold test and therefore is considered to be Late Silurian in age. The corresponding pole (12‡S, 340‡S) is concordant with the Ludlovian segment of the apparent polar wander path for Baltica. This result does not support hypotheses about significant post-Caledonian dextral tectonic movements along the TESZ. Tectonic movements and accretion of blocks along the SW edge of Baltica must have occurred before the latest Silurian. ß 2000 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved. inian. Przybylowicz and Stupnicka [30] correlate the Upper Ludlowian Niewachlo¤w grey- wackes with the diabase sills. Sampling Only two exposures of the diabase intrusion are available in the HCM. Two sites consisting of 20 samples were collected in the Pragowiec Ravine near the village of Bardo, on the northern limb of the Bardo syncline. In both localities the earlier described [25] contact of dia- base bodies with Silurian sedimentary rocks is not exposed at present. The bedding (strike and dip) of Silurian shales and greywackes was measured in several sites located in the vicinity of studied outcrops. We calculate a mean paleomagnetic pole from each of the laboratories’ datasets and combine these with a previously determined pole from correlative rocks in Yunnan [‘N1’ of Zhang and Piper, Precambrian Res. 85 (1997) 173–199], to obtain an overall weighted mean paleomagnetic pole (04.4 ° N, 161.1° E, A95=12.9° , Q=7) for the South China block at 748 ± 12 Ma. The combined ‘Z1’ pole is considered to be primary based on its thermal stability, its magnetostratigraphic consistency, and a soft-sediment fold test determined by previous work. We calculate a mean paleomagnetic pole from each of the laboratories’ datasets and combine these with a previously determined pole from correlative rocks in Yunnan [‘N1’ of Zhang and Piper, Precambrian Res. 85 (1997) 173–199], to obtain an overall weighted mean paleomagnetic pole (04.4 ° N, 161.1° E, A95=12.9° , Q=7) for the South China block at 748 ± 12 Ma. The combined ‘Z1’ pole is considered to be primary based on its thermal stability, its magnetostratigraphic consistency, and a soft-sediment fold test determined by previous work. Results from individual sampling areas constrain the depositional paleolatitude of the Liantuo Formation and equivalent Sinian rocks to 30– 40° . This result applies to one or both of the stratigraphically adjacent Chang’an and Nantuo glacial deposits; unfortunately, it is neither high nor low enough to refute any of the conceptual models for the enigmatic Neoproterozoic glaciations. The new basal Sinian paleopole, in the context of recent paleomagnetic and geochronological results from Australia, suggests that the Nantuo glaciation is pre-Marinoan. This has come, in part, from recognition of the important and enig- matic changes in the biosphere during these times (Knoll and Walter, 1992; Dalziel et al., 1994). This interest has also prompted a re-evaluation of Neoproterozoic glaciation because glacial rocks of this age are often a part of distinctive facies associations; the diamictites frequently occur interbedded with rocks more often assigned to low latitudes such as carbonates, red beds and phos- phorites (Schemerhorn, 1974; Hambrey and Harland, 1981; Harland, 1983; Fairchild et al., 1994). This debate has a bearing on such questions as the obliquity of the Earth during Neoproterozoic times (e.g. Williams, 1993). A recent palaeomagnetic study of ~600Ma Marinoan periglacial rocks in South Australia has established unequivocally that they were formed close to the ancient equator as defined by the axial geocentric dipole model (Schmidt and Williams, 1995).

3-199 1. Introduction The last few years have seen a heightened interest in the Neoproterozoic Earth. This has come, in part, from recognition of the important and enig- matic changes in the biosphere during these times (Knoll and Walter, 1992; Dalziel et al., 1994). This interest has also prompted a re-evaluation of Neoproterozoic glaciation because glacial rocks of this age are often a part of distinctive facies associations; the diamictites frequently occur interbedded with rocks more often assigned to low latitudes such as carbonates, red beds and phos- phorites (Schemerhorn, 1974; Hambrey and Harland, 1981; Harland, 1983; Fairchild et al., 1994). Whether or not lowland ice sheets actually occu- pied latitudes much lower than Permo- Carboniferous and Quaternary ice has, however, been the subject of much recent debate (e.g. Meert and Van der Voo, 1994; Williams et al., 1995; Young, 1995). This debate has a bearing on such questions as the obliquity of the Earth during Neoproterozoic times (e.g. Williams, 1993). A recent palaeomagnetic study of ~600Ma Marinoan periglacial rocks in South Australia has established unequivocally that they were formed close to the ancient equator as defined by the axial geocentric dipole model (Schmidt and Williams, 1995).

At this point, the applied field value defines the coercivity of the remanence (Her). The peak field in the pulse demagnetizer is unable to fully saturate haematite although it is adequate to identify the essential behaviour of this mineral. The acquisition of IRM is best described by a combination of curves of cumulative log Gaussian (CLG) functions. Curves are observed to be a combi- nation of at least two cumulative functions in the Sinian red sediments. Furthermore, the paleolatitudes indicate that both magnetizations must date from the early Paleozoic. The available constraints lead us to prefer the interpretation that the Liberty Hills Formation carries a primary rem- anence. The similarity of the Nash Hills and Frazier Ridge poles is generally interpreted as supporting the integrity of the data sets. Not only do they have similar pole positions but they also have similar magnetic propertiesÐin both cases the remanence is held solely by a hematite carrier, and both record all sites with the same polarity. However, the Nash Hills pole is based on only 12 samples from par- tially remagnetized red calcareous siltstones of un- certain stratigraphic position. No correlative red calcareous sedimentary rocks were observed in the EWM during this study, and the age of the Nash Hills samples is therefore unknown. It is possible, therefore, that there could be a time gap between the deposition of the Frazier Ridge Formation and the Nash Hills siltstones, and the similarity of the magnetizations may indicate a regional early Pa- leozoic remagnetization event. Watts and Bramall (1981), using data from the Late Cambrian sedimentary rocks of the Frazier Ridge Formation in the Ellsworth Mountains, suggested an approximate 807 counter- clockwise rotation of the EWM. This pole position and the tectonic interpretation are supported by data from 12 samples analyzed from undated sed- imentary rocks in the Nash Hills, some 250 km south of the Ellsworth Mountains themselves (Gru- now et al. 1987). Grunow et al. (1987), based on data from Middle Jurassic granitoids, suggested a 157 counterclockwise rotation of the EWM, post- dating the acquisition of the primary remanence. Together, the three poles have been interpreted as supporting a prebreakup position close to southern Africa. This article presents a new, well-de®ned, and dated pole from the late Middle to possibly early Late Cambrian Liberty Hills Formation in the southern Ellsworth Mountains. Using this pole in conjunction with geologic evidence, we assess the validity of the available paleomagnetic data and the reconstruction models for the EWM within Gondwana. view that the Ellsworth Mountains are part of a microplateÐthe Ellsworth-Whitmore Mountains crustal blockÐthat rotated independently of the main Gondwana continental blocks during breakup. The Liberty Hills pole differs from both previous poles recovered from Cambrian rocks in the Ellsworth Mountains and from the available Gondwana reference pole data. Our pole indicates a more northerly prebreakup position for the Ellsworth Mountains than previously suggested, contradicting the overwhelming geologic evidence for a prebreakup position close to southern Africa. Watts and Bramall (1981), using data from the Late Cambrian sedimentary rocks of the Frazier Ridge Formation in the Ellsworth Mountains, suggested an approximate 807 counter- clockwise rotation of the EWM. This pole position and the tectonic interpretation are supported by data from 12 samples analyzed from undated sed- imentary rocks in the Nash Hills, some 250 km south of the Ellsworth Mountains themselves (Gru- now et al. 1987). Grunow et al. (1987), based on data from Middle Jurassic granitoids, suggested a 157 counterclockwise rotation of the EWM, post- dating the acquisition of the primary remanence. Together, the three poles have been interpreted as supporting a prebreakup position close to southern Africa. This article presents a new, well-de®ned, and dated pole from the late Middle to possibly early Late Cambrian Liberty Hills Formation in the southern Ellsworth Mountains. Using this pole in conjunction with geologic evidence, we assess the validity of the available paleomagnetic data and the reconstruction models for the EWM within Gondwana.
