The younger Viljuy aulacogen (®g. 2), consisting of the Viljuy (G1) and Ygyatinsky (G2) grabens, extends westward »600 km into the Siberian Plate (Zonenshain et al. 1990). Analysis of paleomagnetic data (Gurevich 1984; Pavlov and Pe- trov 1996, 1997; Smethurst et al. 1998) suggests a counterclockwise rotation of the portion of the Si- berian Plate north of the Viljuy aulacogen relative to that south of the aulacogen in the mid-Paleozoic (Wenlock-Esmian: 0.43±0.39 Ga). Smethurst et al. (1998) estimated a rotation of »207 about a rotation pole at 607N, 1007E, just west of the basin. Proterozoic diabase dikes are abundant in the main areas of exposed basement in the Siberian Plate and in Riphean and Vendian cover rocks (Ernst et al. 1996 and references therein). In an ear- lier study, those in and adjacent to the Anabar Shield were divided into 10 swarms on the basis of trend, location, composition, and K-Ar age (®g. 3; Okrugin et al. 1990). Five of these swarms occur in the general area of this study. The east-trending Kuonamka swarm (K-Ar ages of 1600±1200 Ma), the southeast-trending East Anabar swarm (K-Ar ages of ca. 1700 Ma), and the east-northeast-trending Central Anabar swarm (K-Ar ages of 1800±1400 Ma) intrude highly metamorphosed Archea

The east-trending Kuonamka swarm (K-Ar ages of 1600±1200 Ma), the southeast-trending East Anabar swarm (K-Ar ages of ca. 1700 Ma), and the east-northeast-trending Central Anabar swarm (K-Ar ages of 1800±1400 Ma) intrude highly metamorphosed Archean rocks and, occasionally, Early Riphean rocks. The Chieress swarm (K-Ar ages of ca. 1200±900 Ma) and the Ju- ken swarm (K-Ar ages of 1300±1200 Ma), both of east-southeast trend, cut Early Riphean cover rocks immediately to the east of the Anabar Shield. Assuming that the Siberian Plate has remained intact since the Mesopro- terozoic, except for mid-Paleozoic opening of the Viljuy Rift, then the above results indicate that the Siberian Plate was in low latitudes at ca. 1503 and 1384 Ma, broadly similar to low latitudes determined for Laurentia from well- dated paleopoles at 1460±1420, 1320±1290, and 1267 Ma. This would allow Laurentia and Siberia to have been attached in the Mesoproterozoic, as suggested in several recent studies based on geological criteria. However, because paleo- magnetic results from the Anabar Shield region do not average out secular variation and the ages of poles from Siberia and Laurentia are not well matched, it is not yet possible to distinguish between these reconstructions or to rule out other con®gurations that also maintain the two cratons at low paleolatitudes. Analysis of paleomagnetic data (Gurevich 1984; Pavlov and Pe- trov 1996, 1997; Smethurst et al. 1998) suggests a counterclockwise rotation of the portion of the Si- berian Plate north of the Viljuy aulacogen relative to that south of the aulacogen in the mid-Paleozoic (Wenlock-Esmian: 0.43±0.39 Ga). The pioneering work of R.G. McConnell remains the most complete de - scription, and with only minor changes, the basic framework for the alluvial deposits of the Klondike goldfields. d Both hypotheses A and B indicate that Lower White Channel gravel was deposited by at least the Gauss chron (>2.58 Ma). However, the assignment of a Gauss versus Olduvai age for the Upper White Channel and Klondike gravel units is difficult on the basis of paleomagnetic data alone. A Gauss age for the Upper White Channel – Klondike gravel magnetopolarity zone is preferred for the following reasons. (1) Evidence from elsewhere in the northern Cordillera (Westgate et al. 1990; Duk-Rodkin et al. 1996; Barendregt et al. 1996), indicates that full-glacial conditions likely existed in the northern Cordillera prior to the Olduvai (>1.77 Ma). Ma to <780 ka, including the Jaramillo subchron (1.1 Ma). ted in this paper, we have analyzed the paleomagnetism of the Siwalik Group at Tinau Khola and Surai Khola, and the Dumri Formation along Tansen road (Fig. 1). Complete results will be reported elsewhere, but we report here observations on lithologic control of paleomagnetism. Our pilot set of samples focused on three rock types: sand- stone, laminated siltstone, and paleosol (i.e., mas- sive, pedoturbated and bioturbated siltstone). Our results show that paleosols (Fig. 3, A–C) and sandstones (Fig. 3, D–F) have erratic thermal demagnetization behaviors. The few sandy silt- stones that were sampled showed more coherent behavior. In contrast, thermal demagnetization of samples from laminated siltstone (Fig. 4) dis- played coherent demagnetization trajectories, many without significant directional changes dur- ing thermal demagnetization. Our results show that wherever possible in the Siwalik Group of Nepal, laminated siltstone should be sampled for paleomagnetic studies, and we have exclusively focused the remainder of our paleomagnetic sam- pling on laminated siltstones. PALEOMAGNETISM IN KHUTIA KHOLA DEPOSITS Following initial NRM measurements, at least three samples from each site at Khutia Khola were subjected to progressive thermal demag- netization. A wide range of thermal demagnetiz- ation behaviors was observed, as seen in vector end-point diagrams (Zijderveld, 1967) (Fig. 4). Unblocking temperatures for almost all finely laminated siltstone samples are mainly above 600 °C, indicating that hematite is the dominant carrier of NRM. For most samples, thermal de- magnetization reveals essentially univectorial de- cay of NRM toward the origin of the vector end- point diagram (e.g., Fig. 4, B–E). A minority of samples showed evidence of a low unblocking temperature component approximately aligned with the present geomagnetic field. Principal component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980) of NRM remaining at four to six successive temperature steps generally above 600 °C was used to deter- mine the characteristic remanent magnetism (ChRM) component. sper- sion (angular standard deviation) of virtual geo- magnetic poles (VGPs) for the class A sites is 14.4°, which compares closely to the 13.5° value compiled for rocks with ages to 5 Ma between lat 20° and 30° by Merrill and McElhinny (1983). This observation suggests complete sampling of geomagnetic secular variation and indicates that the time interval of NRM acquisition was short compared with the few thousands of years of dominant periodicities of secular variation. Tauxe and Kent (1984) provided strong arguments that the NRM of similar sedimentary rocks in the Siwalik Group of Pakistan was a depositional remanent magnetism carried by hematite and was acquired essentially at the time of deposition. Our observation of significant shallowing of the mean inclination of ChRM compared with the expected geomagnetic field direction at the time of deposition (see following) provides further evidence for a depositional origin of the ChRM in the Siwalik Group of Khutia Khola. Ion microprobe U–Pb dating of zircon and baddeleyite indicates that the MDS was emplaced at 755± 3M a( 9 5% conﬁdence interval ) and palaeomagnetic results conﬁrm that the swarm is equivalent in age to dykes of the Northampton Inlier. Li * Tectonics Special Research Centre, Department of Geology and Geophysics, The University of Western Australia, Nedlands, W A 6907, Australia Abstract An interpreted primary magnetic remanence that passed a fold test has been revealed from six sampling sites in the pink ‘cap dolomite’ of the Neoproterozoic Walsh Tillite, southern Kimberley, northwestern Australia. A palaeomagnetic pole ( WTC ) at (21.5 ° S, 282.4° E) with dp =12.2° and dm=15.4° , based on results of the ﬁve best sites, gives a palaeolatitude of 45 ± 12° for the sampling region, and ca 25 ± 12° for the Adelaide Fold Belt where two Neoproterozoic glaciations occur. This palaeopole falls 58° away from the Marinoan glaciation (the Elatina Formation) pole, and the palaeolatitude for the region studied is around 30 ° higher than that predicted by the Marinoan and younger Neoproterozoic poles from Australia. If the WTC pole is accepted as a palaeopole at the end of the Walsh glaciation, the Walsh Tillite is thus likely to be of Sturtian (ca 770–750 Ma) rather than Marinoan age. A comparison of the revised late Mesoproterozoic to Neoproterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP) for East Gondwana with that of Laurentia suggests that supercontinent Rodinia broke apart by about 750 Ma, after the Sturtian glaciation. If the WTC pole is accepted as a palaeopole at the end of the Walsh glaciation, the Walsh Tillite is thus likely to be of Sturtian (ca 770–750 Ma) rather than Marinoan age. A comparison of the revised late Mesoproterozoic to Neoproterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP) for East Gondwana with that of Laurentia suggests that supercontinent Rodinia broke apart by about 750 Ma, after the Sturtian glaciation. The new data do not discriminate between the snowball Earth model and the high-obliquity Earth model for the Neoproterozoic time. The Abadeh Section The so-called Abadeh section (latitude 30ø54'N and longitude 53ø13'E; Figure 1) is located in the province of Fars, about 260 km south of Esfahan and 60 km southeast of the city of Abadeh. The sequence crops out in the Hambast Range at an altitude of -2000 m. The Uppermost Permian consists of the Hambast Formation, which has a thickness of 34 m in our section (Figure 2). The lower part of the Hambast Formation comprises a 17-m-thick alternating sequence of tens of centimeter thick greyish to black limestone beds and shales (unit 6 [IJRG, 1981]), while the upper part consist

er part consists of reddish nodular and thin bedded limestones of ammonitico rosso type (unit 7 [IJRG, 1981]). After a distinct lithologic change, sedimentation resumed during the Lower Triassic first with a short shaly interval (30 cm of so-called Transition beds) followed by the thin bedded \"en plaquettes\" pale greyish limestones and shales of the Elikah Formation. This latter formation is very thick (several hundred meters) and forms cliffs in the landscape. The thin interval of stromatolites (algal biolithites) at the base of the Elikah Formation is interpreted as regressive shallow water deposits by IJRG [1981]. B2, PAGES 2805-2815, FEBRUARY 10, 2000 New constraints on the Upper Permian and Lower Triassic geomagnetic polarity timescale from the A badeh section (central Iran) Yves Gallet, 1 Leopold Krystyn, 2 Jean Besse, and Luc-Emmanuel Ricou 1 1 Abdolah Saidi, 3 Abstract. We present the magnetostratigraphy of the Abadeh section (central Iran). Thermal demagnetization shows two magnetic components: one at low unblocking temperatures, which corresponds to a present day-field direction, and another at high temperatures. This second component, which contains both polarities, is interpreted as a primary magnetization acquired during sediment deposition at a paleolatitude of about 7.7øS. A sequence of 14 magnetic polarity zones is obtained in the intervals during the Upper Dzhulfian-Lower Changhsingian (Upper Permian) and during the Griesbachian (Lower Triassic). Combining data from south China, Canada, Pakistan, and Iran, we propose a composite (but still uncomplete) Upper Permian and Lower Triassic geomagnetic polarity timescale. 1. Cretaceous Kurihashi Granodiorite on the Pacific coast of northeast Japan are divided into two groups based on paleomagnetic data. One group (A) preserves stable single thermoremanent magnetizations (TRM) with large westerly deflected declinations. The other group (B) has two or three distinct components of natural remanent magnetization (NRM): components with high, middle, and low unblocking temperatures show westerly declinations (nearly identical with the stable TRM directions of group A), as well as northerly and easterly declinations. Rock magnetic experiments indicate that the dominant magnetic mineral of both groups is Ti-poor titanomagnetite. Group A samples contain superparamagnetic (SP) titanomagnetite because they show a frequency dependence with the initial susceptibility measurements: Hysteresis parameters of group B samples are consistent with a mixture of single-domain (SD) and multidomain (MD) grains. Electron microscopy confirms the presence of MD size magnetite in the group B samples. Fission track thermochronology indicates that the Kurihashi Granodiorite underwent a post cooling hydrothermal event during the Late Cretaceous; thus the northerly and easterly NRM components seem to have a thermoviscous origin. Group A samples contain superparamagnetic (SP) titanomagnetite because they show a frequency dependence with the initial susceptibility measurements: Hysteresis parameters of group B samples are consistent with a mixture of single-domain (SD) and multidomain (MD) grains. Electron microscopy confirms the presence of MD size magnetite in the group B samples. Fission track thermochronology indicates that the Kurihashi Granodiorite underwent a post cooling hydrothermal event during the Late Cretaceous; thus the northerly and easterly NRM components seem to have a thermoviscous origin. Many samples have anomalously high unblocking temperatures (up to 560øC) compared to predictions of SD theory and probably result from long thermal demagnetization \"tails\" of thermoviscous remanent magnetizations (TVRM) carried by MD magnetite. A strong TVRM was acquired during the hydrothermal event and is correlated with the long normal-polarity superchron of the geomagnetic field. Because highly oblique (left-lateral) subduction was active along the eastern Eurasian margin during the same period, the primary TRM and TVRM components record counterclockwise rotation (-120 ø) of the Kurihashi Granodiorite and remarkable wrench deformation along the continental margin. 1. Determination of the timing and extent of rotational events based on reliable paleomagnetic data and radiometric ages is essential to clarify the tectonic history of the Eurasian plate margin. In this article, we present a paleomagnetic and chro- nologic study of the Kurihashi Granodiorite near the Pacific coast of northeast Japan. A preliminary investigation [Itoh et al., 1998a] showed that the plutonic rock can be divided into two groups based on paleomagnetic data: one sample group (A) preserves a stable single component of thermoremanent magnetization (TRM), and the other sample group (B) has two or three distinct components of remanence. The mean char- acteristic direction of the TRMs of group A has a large west- erly deflection (Figure 2) consistent with other directions re- ported from Cretaceous plutonic rocks in northeast Japan [Ito and Tokieda, 1986]. It is expected therefore that analysis of the multicomponent remanent magnetization will indicate the ro- tational process in our study area. In addition, fission track thermochronology will provide us with the timing of rema- nence acquisition events, namely, the initial cooling of the plutonic body and later thermal event that is anticipated from fracture-filling mineral assemblages lAmario et al., 1998]. The lack of reverse polarity magnetizations in the Berriasian-Barremian series, together with their distinct hysteresis properties that are typical of remagnetized carbonates elsewhere, are taken as evidence for a secondary overprint in the lower part of the succession. Migration of fluids [e.g., Ge and Garven, 1992] expelled or derived from orogenic belts is regarded as a possible mechanism of remagnetization because the circumstantial spatial and tempo- ral association with secondary magnetizations, although often no direct geochemical characterization of the fluid can be made. A burial diagenetic origin for a secondary magnetization has re- cently been described for some North American Pennsylvanian carbonate rocks [Banerjee et al., 1997] and is supported by oxy- gen isotope ratios in their authigenic magnetites [Ripperdan et al., 1998].
